issues.legal_issue: A purchaser seeking specific performance of a contract requiring payment must prove continuous readiness and willingness, including the ability to pay or timely arrange the balance consideration.
material_facts: The purchaser alleged an agreement to buy immovable property and pleaded that he was ready and willing to perform.
The agreement required payment of the balance consideration by a specified date, but the purchaser gave no cogent evidence that he had funds or timely arrangements to obtain them.
The purchaser’s financial records showed that he lacked sufficient funds when performance was due.
The purchaser deposited the balance consideration in court only years after the contractual performance date.
The lower courts relied on a general observation about the purchaser’s business and presumed sources of funds without adequately examining the evidence of his financial capacity.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser failed to prove continuous readiness and willingness, particularly his readiness to pay the balance consideration, and was not entitled to specific performance. The lower courts’ decrees granting that relief were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as it stood before the 2018 amendment, a plaintiff must plead and prove performance or continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract, except terms prevented or waived by the defendant. Under the explanations to Section 16(c), actual tender or court deposit is generally unnecessary, but the plaintiff must show that funds were available or could be arranged in time. Readiness concerns capacity, including financial capacity; willingness concerns conduct. The assessment considers the plaintiff’s conduct and the evidence throughout the proceedings, and a later court deposit alone does not prove readiness at the time performance was due. The Court relied on Man Kaur v. Hartar Singh Sangha, Pt. Prem Raj v. D.L.F. Housing and Construction (Private) Ltd., N.P. Thirugnanam v. Dr. R. Jagan Mohan Rao, Umabai v. Nilkanth Dhondiba Chavan, His Holiness Acharya Swami Ganesh Dassji v. Sita Ram Thapar, and Kalawati v. Rakesh Kumar.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and monetary_obligation_due and (insufficient_funds_at_performance_time or no_proof_of_funds_or_timely_arrangements) and not continuous_readiness_proven

predicates.specific_performance_claim: A purchaser seeks an order requiring completion of an agreement to sell.
predicates.monetary_obligation_due: The purchaser's contractual performance requires payment of the remaining purchase money by the time fixed for performance.
predicates.insufficient_funds_at_performance_time: The evidence shows that the purchaser lacked sufficient funds when payment was due.
predicates.no_proof_of_funds_or_timely_arrangements: The purchaser provides no cogent evidence that funds were available or could be arranged in time to make the required payment.
predicates.continuous_readiness_proven: The purchaser establishes by evidence continuous readiness and willingness to perform the purchaser's essential contractual obligations.

issues.definition: When a purchaser seeks specific performance of a contract requiring payment and fails to establish continuous readiness, including funds or timely arrangements to pay, specific performance is refused.

issues.legal_issue: Filing a suit for specific performance within the limitation period does not by itself entitle a purchaser to the remedy when the agreed performance timeframe and the parties’ conduct make equitable relief inappropriate.
material_facts: The agreement specified a time for completing the sale, but the purchaser filed suit nearly three years after the contractual performance date and shortly before the limitation period expired.
The purchaser had paid only a small advance relative to the agreed sale consideration.
The property had undergone a substantial rise in value, and the purchaser had not shown that the seller caused the delay or that the purchaser was financially ready when performance was due.
issues.conclusion: The suit’s filing within the limitation period did not by itself justify specific performance; the agreed timeframe, delay, conduct, and surrounding circumstances remained relevant to the court’s discretion.
issues.legal_principle: Specific performance is discretionary. The absence of a general presumption that time is of the essence in contracts for the sale of immovable property does not make contractual time limits irrelevant; the court considers the contract’s terms, the property, surrounding circumstances, and the parties’ conduct. A suit filed within limitation need not be decreed automatically, particularly where the purchaser delayed after the performance date and the circumstances make enforcement inequitable. The Court relied on Sections 10 and 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as then applicable, and on Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani, K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan, Azhar Sultana v. B. Rajamani, and Saradamani Kandappan v. S. Rajalakshmi.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and contractual_performance_timeframe and substantial_delay_after_performance_date and (small_advance_paid or substantial_property_value_rise)

predicates.specific_performance_claim: A purchaser seeks an order requiring completion of an agreement to sell.
predicates.contractual_performance_timeframe: The agreement sets a timeframe for completing the transaction or taking steps toward completion.
predicates.substantial_delay_after_performance_date: The purchaser waits substantially after the agreed performance date before bringing the claim or pursuing completion.
predicates.small_advance_paid: The purchaser has paid only a small part of the agreed consideration in advance.
predicates.substantial_property_value_rise: The property has substantially increased in value during the delay.

issues.definition: Where a purchaser seeks specific performance after substantial delay under an agreement with a performance timeframe, a small advance or substantial increase in property value means that filing within limitation does not make specific performance automatic.
